headline: Highest risk is compliance/data leakage: EMQX handles IoT data and broad egress, while the content-writing agent can also egress broadly, creating a default path for sensitive data to leave the workspace.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared channel is documented, so direct prompt injection is not established. However, both agents have broad network egress, and B exposes an HTTP API, so if A’s content is manually or programmatically fed into B, attacker-controlled text could influence downstream handling. The pathway is plausible but not default.
conditions: IF A’s output is copied into B’s HTTP API payloads without sanitization
IF a shared message queue or clipboard is introduced between A and B
mitigations: Add a one-line content filter before B ingests A’s text
Disable any automatic forwarding from A to B
Use a fixed schema for B inputs instead of free text
Log and review the first 10 cross-agent messages
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all A→B content

B_data_leakage.rationale: B explicitly touches IoT data and has HTTP API/network egress, while A also has broad network egress. Even without a shared workspace, the pair creates a plausible default leakage path if either agent receives sensitive IoT content and forwards it outward. The evidence is indirect, so I choose medium rather than low.
conditions: IF IoT data is supplied to B and B forwards it over HTTP
IF A is given any sensitive content and relays it to external services
mitigations: Restrict B to non-sensitive test data for a quick trial
Turn off outbound network access on A during evaluation
Mask identifiers before any A→B transfer
Review B’s HTTP destinations before enabling production
requires-engineering: enforce per-field redaction at the API boundary

C_capability_conflict.rationale: The profiles show overlapping broad network egress, but no shared writable filesystem, git state, or OAuth scopes. That makes direct capability conflict possible only if an operator wires both agents to the same mutable resource. With current profiles, the overlap is limited and the blast radius is small.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable HTTP endpoint
IF an operator gives both agents write access to the same external resource
mitigations: Assign separate endpoints for A and B
Keep one agent read-only during testing
Document which agent owns each API
Check for duplicate writes in the first run
requires-engineering: add locking or idempotency keys

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a content-writing agent and B is an email-scheduling agent with HTTP API access, so A’s output could become B’s input and then be acted on. There is no documented verification step, and the pair could propagate incorrect content into scheduled communications. This is plausible in default orchestration, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF A’s generated text is used as B’s scheduling or message content
IF B sends or schedules messages without human review
mitigations: Insert a human approval step before B acts
Require B to validate A’s output against a template
Limit A to drafting only, not final copy
Run one dry-run with dummy recipients
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking before send

E_compliance.rationale: B touches IoT data and has broad egress, while A also has broad egress. That creates a compliance risk if regulated IoT or personal data is routed through either agent without residency or retention controls. The profiles do not show a specific residency mismatch, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is processed by B
IF either agent stores or forwards data outside the required jurisdiction
mitigations: Confirm the data class before enabling either agent
Keep regulated data out of A entirely
Review retention settings on B
Disable external logging for a test run
requires-engineering: add residency and retention policy enforcement
